comments.author: spudlyo
comments.text:
You can hire a grandmaster-level software engineer, leave them pretty much alone, and trust that they will start making valuable contributions to long-term projects and will reliably be making your software system better.


This statement struck me as profoundly wrongheaded and naive. In my experience, there is little correlation between being good at programming and being motivated to produce valuable contributions to an existing codebase -- if anything it's the opposite. There is a huge amount of friction to overcome when learning to work in a new software system, and the better programmer you are, the more likely you are to find someone else's code objectionable. I've known many first-class programmers who were terrible procrastinators, and have largely gotten away with it because they could quickly produce the necessary code by deadline.

comments.author: andrewballinger
comments.text:
Grandmaster-level software engineers have a broader skill set then you're counting here and meet the description in the article.

I encourage these people to not vibe-code, but rather vibe-write-documentation, vibe-understand-requirements, and vibe-soften-their-MRs, which can also help those individuals perform at a higher level.

comments.author: twitchard
comments.text: Yes there are definitely people who are "grandmaster-level" at something smaller than the task of shipping valuable software as part of a team. If you need to be steered in order to produce valuable contributions, then you remain competitive as long as you produce more marginal value per unit of steering than the AI does. "Brilliant but needs guidance" is going to be the engineering archetype that suffers most, because that unfortunately seems to be profile that these AI coding agents occupy also.

comments.author: kornel
comments.text: That statement entirely depends on the unstated definition of what a grandmaster-level software engineer is. It could have been defined (tautologically) as someone who has good judgement about which contributions are valuable for the end goal, and deliver them instead of aimlessly programming clever things.

comments.author: kornel
comments.text:
The problem is that agentic coding is heading towards scaling by dumb brute force. We don't have technology to create an AI Shakespeare, but we're racing to build data centers of Infinite Monkeys instead (seriously, research into smarter models hasn't moved past optimizing transformers, but efficiency and speed improvements are going well).

I have a pessimistic view that the VCs funding the AI craze are primarily interested in removing their weakness of depending on human labor, even if the results are worse. They don't want Centaurs, they want minions.

For any LLM problem the solution will be throwing more LLMs at it. Unmaintainable code? Just generate new one. Generate 50 or 1000 new versions and send minions to try which version is least buggy. Insecure? Deploy minions to patch holes faster than the minions of your adversary can exploit them.

comments.author: kghose
comments.text:

comments.author: wrs
comments.text: I recently ran across the idea of a transition to "product pods", basically like ordinary corporate software teams but smaller and with a different role ratio, more like one product manager + one QA manager + two developers. The theory is that with AI assistance in all the roles, two developers can keep up with all the ideas from one product manager, and it'll take a full-time QA person to maintain whatever process is necessary for the codebase to stay sane. Or maybe the numbers aren't quite right, or maybe it won't work at all — but at least it seemed like a coherent thing to try.
